Prove the validity of the decomposition theorem for polyhedra by showing that
every polyhedron P admits the representation P = {x+c : x ∈X, c ∈C}, for some polytope
X and some polyhedral cone C.
Solution: Decomposition Theorem for Polyhedra
Theorem 1 (Decomposition Theorem). Every polyhedron P ⊆Rn admits a representation
P = {x + c : x ∈X, c ∈C} = X + C
where X is a polytope and C is a polyhedral cone.
Definition 1.
• A polyhedron is a set P = {x ∈Rn : Ax ≤b} for some matrix
A ∈Rm×n and vector b ∈Rm.
• A polytope is a bounded polyhedron.
• A polyhedral cone is a set C = {x ∈Rn : Ax ≤0} for some matrix A.
• The recession cone of P is CP = {d ∈Rn : x + λd ∈P for all x ∈P, λ ≥0}.
Lemma 1. If P = {x : Ax ≤b} is a nonempty polyhedron, then its recession cone is
CP = {d : Ad ≤0}
which is a polyhedral cone.
Proof. Let d ∈CP. Then for any x ∈P and λ ≥0, we have x + λd ∈P, which means
A(x + λd) ≤b.
Since Ax ≤b, this gives λAd ≤0 for all λ ≥0. This implies Ad ≤0.
Conversely, suppose Ad ≤0. For any x ∈P with Ax ≤b and any λ ≥0:
A(x + λd) = Ax + λAd ≤b + λ · 0 = b
Thus x + λd ∈P for all x ∈P and λ ≥0, so d ∈CP.
Therefore CP = {d : Ad ≤0} is a polyhedral cone.
Lemma 2. The set X = P ∩{x : ∥x∥≤r} for sufficiently large r contains all extreme
points of P.
Proof. By the Minkowski-Weyl theorem, P has finitely many extreme points v1, . . . , vk.
Choose r > maxi=1,...,k ∥vi∥. Then all extreme points lie in the ball of radius r.
Proof. Let P = {x : Ax ≤b} be a nonempty polyhedron. We construct the decomposition
in several steps.
Step 1: Construct the recession cone.
By Lemma ??, C = CP = {d : Ad ≤0} is a polyhedral cone.
Step 2: Construct the polytope.
1

Choose any point p ∈P. Define
X = (P −C) ∩Br(0)
where Br(0) = {x : ∥x∥≤r} for r sufficiently large, and P −C = {x −c : x ∈P, c ∈C}.
First, note that P −C = {x : Ax ≤b}, since if x ∈P and c ∈C, then
A(x −c) = Ax −Ac ≤b −0 = b
Also, (P −C) ∩Br(0) is bounded (by construction) and is the intersection of polyhedra,
hence a polytope.
Step 3: Alternative construction using extreme representation.
By the Minkowski-Weyl theorem, we can write
P = conv{v1, . . . , vk} + cone{r1, . . . , rℓ}
where vi are the extreme points and rj are the extreme rays of P.
Define:
X = conv{v1, . . . , vk}
C = cone{r1, . . . , rℓ}
Then X is a polytope (convex hull of finitely many points) and C is a polyhedral cone
(positive hull of finitely many vectors).

Step 5: Uniqueness considerations.
Note that while the decomposition exists, it is not unique.
However, C is uniquely

We have shown that every polyhedron P can be decomposed as P = X +C where X is a
polytope and C is a polyhedral cone (the recession cone of P). This decomposition separates
the ”bounded” part (captured by the polytope) from the ”unbounded directions” (captured
by the cone).

fields.explanation: Keep A=[-1],b=0, P=C=[0,infinity), x=0,c=1 and x-c=-1 outside P. The polyhedron is nonempty and C really is its recession cone. The theorem includes nonemptiness, equality with the universal recession-direction condition for all x in P and all t>=0, and failure of P-C=P. It uses real sets and Mathlib pointwise subtraction. The witness -1 is constructed from 0 and 1 via Set.mem_sub.
fields.flaw: The proof claims that for C={d:Ad≤0}, one has P−C={x:Ax≤b}; equivalently, if x∈P and c∈C then x−c∈P.

fields.witness:
A=[-1],b=0: -1∈P-C, -1∉{Ax≤b}

Take n=1, A=[-1], b=0, so P={x:-x≤0}=[0,∞). Then C={d:-d≤0}=[0,∞). Let x=0∈P and c=1∈C. Then x−c=-1∈P−C, but -1∉P since A(-1)=1>0. Thus P−C≠{x:Ax≤b}.
